extracted.intended_audience: crisis managers, public relations practitioners, and researchers in crisis communication/reputation management
extracted.subtask_description: Evidence-based guidelines (Situational Crisis Communication Theory, SCCT) for assessing reputational threat in organizational crises and selecting matched crisis response strategies to protect reputational assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility: prioritize stakeholder safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The first priority in any crisis is to protect stakeholders from harm, not to protect the reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin crisis communication by addressing physical threats with instructing information (what stakeholders must do) and psychological threats with adapting information (coping information, corrective actions, expressions of concern). Expressions of concern are expected and recommended but are not admissions of guilt. Only after stakeholder needs are met should managers turn to reputational concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting information (instructing and adapting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructing information tells stakeholders what they must do to protect themselves from the physical threat; adapting information helps people cope with the psychological threat of the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver instructing information directly or via media (e.g., recalls, sirens). Provide corrective actions to reassure stakeholders and reduce stress. Include expressions of concern for victims as part of adapting information. These elements both meet ethical obligations and help reduce negative affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors shaping reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Three situational factors determine the reputational threat posed by a crisis: (1) initial crisis responsibility, (2) crisis history, and (3) prior relational reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial crisis responsibility equals stakeholder attributions of organizational control for the crisis. Crisis history (having had similar crises) and an unfavorable prior relational reputation intensify attributions and directly increase reputational threat. Use these three factors together to assess threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis type clusters (victim, accidental, intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT identifies three crisis clusters based on attributions of responsibility: (1) victim cluster — very weak attributions (natural disasters, product tampering, rumor); (2) accidental cluster — minimal attributions (technical-error accident, technical-error product harm); (3) intentional cluster — very strong attributions (human-error accident, organizational misdeed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis type functions as a frame that cues stakeholders about causes, control, intent, and whether the organization is responsible. Identifying the crisis type allows prediction of the initial level of attributed responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step evaluation process for reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: determine initial crisis responsibility by identifying crisis type; Step 2: consider intensifying factors (crisis history and prior relationship reputation) to adjust the reputational threat assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A victim crisis can become as threatening as an accidental or intentional crisis when intensifying factors are present. Use the Crisis History and Prior Relationship Reputation propositions to update the threat estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution theory foundations (cause → emotion → behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: People search for causes of negative events and attribute responsibility; the core emotions are anger and sympathy. Attributions of responsibility evoke anger (if organization judged responsible) or sympathy (if not), which motivate behavioral responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the attribution-emotion-behavior link to predict stakeholder reactions: stronger attributions of responsibility increase negative affect and negative behavioral intentions toward the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCCT propositions linking responsibility, affect, reputation, and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of propositions: Crisis Responsibility–Organizational Reputation (more responsibility → lower reputation); Crisis History Proposition (past similar crises → greater attributed responsibility and damage); Prior Relationship Reputation Proposition (poor prior treatment → greater responsibility and damage); Crisis Responsibility–Affect (more responsibility → more anger, less sympathy); Organizational Reputation–Behavior Intention (more negative reputation → less supportive behavioral intentions); Affect–Behavioral Intention (negative affect → less supportive intentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These propositions describe causal pathways that justify matching response strategies to situation. Research provides empirical support for many of these links; use them to anticipate behavioral consequences of reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis response strategy taxonomy (primary and supplemental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary groups based on perceived acceptance of responsibility: (1) denial, (2) diminish, and (3) rebuild. Supplemental strategies include bolstering (reminder, praise, victimage), apology, compensation, excuse, and other corrective actions (adjusting information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary strategies vary by degree of accepting responsibility: denial (no responsibility), diminish (minimize or excuse), rebuild (accept responsibility, compensate/apologize). Supplemental strategies are best used to augment primary strategies and depend on available reputational capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis response strategies have three objectives relative to protecting reputations: (1) shape attributions of the crisis, (2) change perceptions of the organization in crisis, and (3) reduce the negative affect generated by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers may pursue any combination of these objectives. Choose messages/actions that directly address the intended objective(s): e.g., adjusting information and rebuild strategies reduce negative affect; denial seeks to remove attributions of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching response accommodation to reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT recommends that as reputational threat and negative affect increase, crisis managers should utilize crisis response strategies with greater acceptance of responsibility (more accommodative strategies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Table 3 (SCCT recommendations) to select strategy levels. However, do not assume the most accommodative strategy is always best—more accommodative strategies are costlier and research shows excessive accommodation yields no greater reputational benefit and can sometimes worsen perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and boundary conditions affecting strategy choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial resources and other constraints (e.g., media/internet framing) influence which strategies are feasible. If an organization cannot afford the recommended response, choose the next-best, less-expensive strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits: financial constraints may force use of excuse rather than apology. Media framing and online conversation may restrict an organization's ability to establish frames; manage within those constraints or focus on channels where you can influence framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing cues and their role
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis frames (in communication and thought) emphasize certain factors—cues such as whether an external agent caused the crisis, accidental vs intentional, and technical vs human error—that influence attributions of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis managers can attempt to establish or shape frames by emphasizing specific cues in messages. The media and online posters often determine which frame gains salience; effort should be made to present the organization's side to those arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of media and online platforms in establishing frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Most stakeholders learn about crises from news media; thus media framing is critical. For online-centered crises, posts by managers, influential bloggers, critics and victims create frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the organization's frame to the news media; when crises are predominantly online, engage online actors and content to influence framing. If media or internet discussion provides no clear frame, managers have an easier time establishing their own frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bolstering and reminder strategies as supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolstering (praising stakeholders, reminding of past good works, or evoking victimage) offers minimal opportunities to develop reputational assets and is most effective when used as a supplement to primary strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolstering relies on prior goodwill; use praise or reminders only if credible past good works exist. Supplemental bolstering should not replace corrective actions when the reputational threat is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential negative effect of over-accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using overly accommodative strategies when unnecessary can worsen the situation—stakeholders may infer the crisis is worse if the organization responds aggressively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance accommodative responses with situational assessment. Research shows that excessive accommodation can be more costly with no added reputational benefit; choose responses proportionate to assessed responsibility and threat.
